title: THE SLAVE GOD REFUSED TO SEND BACK: THE SHOCKING COMMAND HIDDEN IN THE LAW OF MOSES
paragraphs: THE SLAVE GOD REFUSED TO SEND BACK: THE SHOCKING COMMAND HIDDEN IN THE LAW OF MOSES

When a human being escaped from bondage, God's Law commanded something that could cost a master his property, confront an entire community's conscience, and reveal a truth about freedom that would ultimately find its deepest fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Imagine hearing footsteps behind you.
You have been running for hours. Your lungs are burning. Your legs are trembling. Every unfamiliar sound makes your heart pound.
You are not running toward wealth.
You are not running toward revenge.
You are running because somewhere behind you is a life you cannot bear to return to.
And if someone catches you, you may lose the freedom you have risked everything to find.
Then, just ahead, you see a settlement.
People are watching.
You don't know whether they will welcome you, question you, or drag you back to the person who claims to own you.
You expect the worst.

After all, throughout much of human history, the powerful have written laws to protect their possessions. And in societies where human beings could be treated as property, an escaped slave could become a problem to be solved rather than a person to be protected.
But then someone opens the Law of Moses.
And what it says is almost impossible to believe.

“Thou shalt not deliver unto his master the servant which is escaped from his master unto thee: He shall dwell with thee, even among you, in that place which he shall choose in one of thy gates, where it liketh him best: thou shalt not oppress him.”
— Deuteronomy 23:15–16, King James Version
Read that again.
Do not return him.
Let him live among you.
Let him choose where he wants to live.
Do not oppress him.
In a world where ownership could determine a person's future, this command placed a remarkable restriction on the master's power.
And perhaps the most astonishing part is what the passage does not say.
It does not tell the fugitive to prove that his master was cruel before receiving protection.
It does not instruct the community to negotiate a price for his return.
It does not command him to resume his former position.
Instead, the text explicitly forbids handing him over and grants him a place to live.
But why?
Why would the same Mosaic Law that regulated slavery also protect someone who escaped it?
Was this an ancient humanitarian exception? Was it specifically about a foreign slave fleeing into Israel? Was God revealing something about justice that His people were still learning to understand?
And what does any of this have to do with the man who would one day stand in a synagogue and announce liberty to the captives?
The answer requires us to face something uncomfortable.
The Bible does not always describe the world as God ultimately desires it to be.

Sometimes it shows God addressing people inside deeply flawed human systems, restraining evil, protecting the vulnerable, and calling His people toward a righteousness greater than the customs surrounding them.
And if we rush past that tension, we may miss the extraordinary significance of these two verses.
The Hebrew begins with a prohibition:
לֹא־תַסְגִּיר עֶבֶד אֶל־אֲדֹנָיו
Lo-tasgír ‘éved el-adonáv.
“You shall not hand over a slave to his master.”
The verb תַסְגִּיר (tasgír) comes from a Hebrew root associated with shutting up, surrendering, or handing someone over into another's control.
It is a forceful prohibition.
The community is forbidden to deliver the fugitive back into his master's power.

The word עֶבֶד (‘éved) can mean servant or slave, depending on context. It does not automatically describe the modern experience of an employee working voluntarily for wages. In ancient Israel and neighboring societies, the term could describe people in relationships of genuine dependency, bondage, or ownership.
We must not soften the language merely because the subject is uncomfortable.
This passage concerns a person who has escaped from a master.
And the Law says not to surrender him.
Then comes another striking phrase:
בַּמָּקוֹם אֲשֶׁר־יִבְחַר
Bammaqóm asher-yivchár.
“In the place that he shall choose.”
Think about that.
A person whose life had been controlled by another is now expressly permitted to choose where to live.
Not where the master chooses.
Not simply where the authorities find it convenient.
Where the fugitive chooses, within the community's towns.
The following words reinforce the point:
בַּטּוֹב לוֹ
Battóv lo.
“Where it is good for him.”
And the command concludes:
לֹא תּוֹנֶנּוּ
Lo tonénnu.
“You shall not mistreat him.”
These are not merely sentimental words.
They impose obligations on the receiving community.
Protection from return.
Permission to reside.
Freedom of settlement.
Protection from mistreatment.
Yet biblical faithfulness requires us to acknowledge a question that serious interpreters have discussed for centuries.
Which escaped slaves did this command protect?
The passage does not explicitly identify the fugitive's nationality or the master's nationality.

Many interpreters understand the law primarily as protecting a slave who fled from a foreign master into Israel. This reading fits the wider setting of Deuteronomy 23, which addresses Israel's relationships with surrounding peoples and the holiness of its community.
Other interpreters understand the wording more broadly, while some Jewish interpretive traditions discuss particular circumstances involving slaves crossing into the land of Israel.
These distinctions matter.
We should not claim that Deuteronomy 23:15–16 explicitly abolished every form of slavery throughout Israel. It did not.
Nor should we pretend that the precise legal scope of the command is beyond dispute.
But the protection actually written in the text remains remarkable.
For the fugitive covered by this law, the community was forbidden to return him to his master.
And to understand why such a command belongs in Israel's Law, we must go backward.
Back to Egypt.
Back to brickmaking.
Back to exhausted bodies and bitter labor.
Back to a people who cried out because their lives were being consumed by oppression.
Exodus 2:23 tells us that the Israelites groaned because of their bondage and cried for help.
Then Exodus 3:7 records God's response:
“I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows.”
Notice the words.
I have seen.
I have heard.
I know.
The God of Israel did not introduce Himself as a distant observer of human suffering.
He revealed Himself as the One who saw the affliction of His people and acted to deliver them.
That does not mean every Israelite law can be reduced to a modern political program. It does mean that Israel's memory of slavery was foundational to its moral identity.
They were repeatedly commanded to remember that they had once been vulnerable foreigners and slaves.
Deuteronomy 24:18 says:
“But thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in Egypt, and the LORD thy God redeemed thee thence: therefore I command thee to do this thing.”
That verse appears in a context requiring justice for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.
The pattern is unmistakable.
Remember your suffering.
Remember your deliverance.
Then refuse to become indifferent to the suffering of others.
Israel was not supposed to forget what oppression felt like simply because Israel was no longer the one under Pharaoh's whip.
And there is something painfully human about that warning.
Because people who have been hurt do not automatically become compassionate.
Sometimes they become protective.
Sometimes suspicious.
Sometimes controlling.
Sometimes the very suffering that should have softened their hearts becomes the justification for hardening them.
A person who once begged for mercy can eventually become someone who refuses to give it.
A person who once needed help can become someone who looks away when another person cries.
A person who once prayed desperately for freedom can become strangely comfortable with another person's bondage.
Perhaps that is why Scripture commands remembrance so often.
Because forgetfulness is not always a failure of memory.
Sometimes it is a failure of love.
And here, in Deuteronomy, the Lord places a boundary around what a community may do to a vulnerable fugitive.
You may not simply hand him back.
You may not mistreat him.
You must allow him a place among you.
It is an ancient command, but its moral challenge reaches across centuries.
What happens when someone else's vulnerability interrupts our comfort?
What happens when protecting someone costs us something?
What happens when mercy demands more than kind words?
It is easy to admire compassion when it remains a beautiful idea.
It is harder when compassion knocks on our door.
But we must also confront the difficult question that cannot be avoided.
If God cared about the enslaved, why did the Law of Moses contain regulations concerning slavery at all?
Why not simply prohibit the institution outright?
This question deserves more than a convenient slogan.

The Old Testament describes several forms of servitude, including debt-related Israelite service and the enslavement of foreigners. These arrangements were not identical, and some were deeply unequal.

Exodus 21 contains laws regulating Hebrew servants and other situations involving slavery. Leviticus 25:44–46 permits Israelites to acquire slaves from surrounding nations and describes certain slaves as inheritable property.
That is morally disturbing to modern readers, and we should not disguise what those passages say.
The Bible also contains restrictions on mistreatment, protections for particular vulnerable people, and commands that challenged aspects of ancient social practice.
For example, Exodus 21:16 condemns kidnapping a person and selling that person.
Exodus 21:26–27 requires freedom for a slave injured in specified ways by a master.
Deuteronomy 23:15–16 protects the fugitive addressed by its command.
These provisions are significant, but they do not erase the existence of slavery within Israel's legal world.
Nor do they justify claiming that biblical slavery was always harmless or voluntary.
The difficult truth is that the Mosaic Law operated within an ancient social setting in which slavery existed.
Christians have offered different explanations for why God permitted certain institutions to be regulated rather than immediately prohibited.
One important interpretive connection comes from Jesus' discussion of divorce in Matthew 19:8.
When questioned about Moses' permission concerning divorce, Jesus explained:
“Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.”
Jesus was speaking specifically about divorce, not directly explaining every Old Testament slavery law.
We must respect that distinction.
Nevertheless, His words reveal an important biblical principle: a legal permission within a fallen society does not necessarily express God's original ideal for human relationships.
To discover that ideal, Jesus pointed His listeners back to creation.
And creation begins with an astonishing declaration.
Genesis 1:27 says:
“So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.”
Before any empire existed, before any human being claimed ownership of another, before anyone had a title, a fortune, or a position of power, humanity was created in God's image.
That dignity was not awarded by a government.
It was not purchased.
It was not earned.
It was bestowed by the Creator.
Every human being bears a dignity that no earthly master has the authority to erase.
This truth does not mean every biblical law immediately applied the full social implications of human equality.
History shows that even people who possessed Scripture often failed to recognize those implications.
Christians themselves have sometimes defended slavery by appealing selectively to biblical passages.
Other Christians, including many abolitionists, appealed to the biblical teaching about God's image, justice, neighbor-love, and freedom in Christ to oppose slavery.
We should remember both realities.
The Bible must not become a weapon for excusing cruelty.
And neither should we force it to say something a particular passage does not say.
Faithfulness requires the courage to read the whole counsel of Scripture, including the verses that make us uncomfortable.
But the story does not end in Deuteronomy.
Centuries later, another man would enter a synagogue in Nazareth.
He would stand to read from the prophet Isaiah.
And His announcement would reach far beyond one escaped slave, one community, or one ancient legal protection.
Luke 4:18 records Jesus declaring:

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised.”
The underlying Greek includes the word:
ἄφεσις — áphesis.
Release.
Liberation.
Remission.
A word used in the New Testament for forgiveness and release.
Jesus was announcing the fulfillment of Isaiah's promise in Himself.
His ministry brought good news to the poor, hope to the oppressed, and the saving reign of God into a world disfigured by sin.
His announcement should not be reduced to political emancipation alone, nor should its concern for suffering people be spiritualized away.
Jesus came to address humanity's deepest bondage to sin and death, and His kingdom calls His followers to love their neighbors with concrete mercy and justice.
Then, in John 8:34, He identified a captivity that reaches into every human heart:
“Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.”
And in John 8:36:
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.”
Here is where the story becomes personal.
Because you may never have run from an earthly master.
You may never have stood at the border of a strange town, terrified that someone would return you to captivity.
But you may know what it feels like to be trapped.
Trapped in a habit you promised to abandon.
Trapped in shame over something you did years ago.
Trapped in bitterness toward someone who hurt you.
Trapped in the exhausting need to appear strong when your heart is falling apart.
You smile in photographs.
You answer messages.
You go to work.
You attend church.
You tell people you are doing fine.
But there are moments when the noise disappears and the truth becomes impossible to avoid.
You are tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of fighting the same temptation.
Tired of remembering what you wish you could undo.
Tired of wondering whether the person you used to be will always determine the person you are allowed to become.
And somewhere in that exhaustion, you begin to believe a terrible lie.
That your past owns you.
That your worst decision has the final word.
That God may forgive other people, but surely He has grown weary of you.
Listen carefully.
Your sin is real. But it is not a master stronger than Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not pretend that your wrongdoing never happened.
It does not call evil good.
It does not erase the need for repentance, restitution where appropriate, or the consequences that some actions leave behind.
Grace is not permission to continue in darkness.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy calling sinners out of darkness and into the life of His Son.
And the Son of God did not come merely to make captivity more comfortable.
He came to save.
At the cross, Jesus bore the judgment that sinners deserve.
He died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, as the apostle Paul proclaims in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
And through faith in Him, forgiveness is offered to people who could never purchase it with their own righteousness.
This is why the Gospel is so different from mere self-improvement.
Self-improvement tells you to become strong enough to change your story.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ has done what you could never do to save yourself.
You do not climb out of sin by pretending you were never guilty.
You come to the Savior confessing that you need mercy.
You repent.
You believe.
You surrender.
And by God's grace, you begin to walk in newness of life.
There is another biblical story that makes this discussion even more extraordinary.
It concerns an actual enslaved man.
His name was Onesimus.
And his story appears in one of the shortest and most deeply personal letters in the New Testament.
The letter to Philemon.
Onesimus had been associated with Philemon, a Christian slaveholder.
The letter indicates that Onesimus was separated from him, although the precise circumstances are not fully explained.
Many readers have traditionally understood Onesimus as a runaway slave, but the text does not explicitly describe the details of his departure.
Somewhere along the way, Onesimus encountered Paul and became a Christian.
Then Paul wrote to Philemon.
And what Paul said was astonishing within the social world of the Roman Empire.
He appealed to Philemon to receive Onesimus:
“Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved.”
— Philemon 1:16
A brother.
Not merely an economic asset.
Not merely a person defined by his social position.
A beloved brother in Christ.
Paul also wrote:
“If thou count me therefore a partner, receive him as myself.”
— Philemon 1:17
And then Paul offered to assume any debt or wrong that Onesimus owed.
There is a profound picture of Christian reconciliation here.
But we must be careful.
Philemon does not explicitly record whether Onesimus was formally emancipated. Paul does not issue a universal legal decree abolishing Roman slavery in this letter.
What he does is confront Philemon with a relationship that the Gospel has transformed.
The man whom Roman society could regard as property must now be received as a beloved brother.
And once you truly understand that another person is your brother or sister in Christ, you cannot simply continue looking at that person through the eyes of selfish domination.
The Gospel reaches into the heart of human relationships.
It challenges pride.
It challenges cruelty.
It challenges the belief that status makes one person more valuable than another.
And it calls believers to a love that is costly, practical, and truthful.
That is why Paul's words in Galatians 3:28 matter:
“There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.”
Paul was speaking about believers' shared standing in Christ, not claiming that all earthly social distinctions had instantly disappeared.
Yet the spiritual equality he proclaimed has far-reaching moral implications.
No slaveholder is spiritually superior because he owns another person.
No enslaved believer is spiritually inferior because society has placed him beneath someone else.
At the foot of the cross, worldly status cannot purchase a better standing before God.
All come as sinners in need of grace.
All who belong to Christ are received through the same Savior.
And now return, for a moment, to the fugitive in Deuteronomy.
Picture him standing at the entrance to that ancient town.
He has no powerful family to defend him.
No wealth with which to negotiate.
No certainty that strangers will care whether he lives in safety.
He has escaped.
He is vulnerable.
And the Law forbids those receiving him from handing him back.
Do you see the moral challenge?
The command requires the community to recognize a human being whose needs cannot simply be dismissed because another person claims authority over him.
It is not the entire biblical doctrine of freedom.
It is not a complete abolition statute.
It is a particular protection within the Mosaic Law.
But it is a real protection.

And when we read it in the wider biblical story of creation, Exodus, the prophets, Jesus Christ, and the apostles, we encounter a God who commands justice, remembers the afflicted, condemns oppression, and calls His people to love their neighbors.
That should change the way we treat people.
Not only the people whose stories are easy to admire.
But the people whose wounds make us uncomfortable.
The person recovering from addiction.
The person rebuilding life after imprisonment.
The person who has fled exploitation.
The person whose reputation was destroyed.
The person who has been abused and is trying to find safety.
The person who walks into church carrying a history everyone else seems eager to discuss.
These situations are not identical to the ancient fugitive slave law, and they require different forms of wisdom and care.
But they raise a question that should trouble every Christian conscience.
When wounded people come near us, do they encounter the compassion of Christ?
Or do they discover another place where their past is used to humiliate them?
We must not confuse mercy with the absence of accountability.
We must not pressure victims to return to unsafe relationships.
We must not use forgiveness as an excuse to protect abusers.
Biblical love does not require us to call evil good.
But neither does biblical holiness give us permission to treat suffering people as disposable.
Jesus never needed to deny the reality of sin in order to show mercy to sinners.
He called people to repentance precisely because He came to save them.
And perhaps that is the truth some of us have spent years avoiding.
We want the mercy of God for ourselves.
But we sometimes want strict judgment for everyone else.
We want Jesus to understand our weaknesses.
But we struggle to extend patience toward another person's struggle.
We want our past covered by grace.
But we keep reopening the wounds of people who are trying to change.
And the Gospel confronts us.
Not to crush us with despair.
But to bring us to repentance.
Because the same Savior who forgives our sins also commands us to love one another.
Maybe you are reading this because you need that mercy today.
Maybe you have been running.
Not from a human master, but from the truth about your own life.
You have been avoiding prayer because you feel ashamed.
Avoiding Scripture because you fear what it might expose.
Avoiding honest conversations because you are exhausted from explaining yourself.
You keep promising that tomorrow will be different.
But tomorrow comes, and the struggle is still there.
And somewhere inside you, a quiet question keeps returning.
Can Jesus still receive someone like me?
Hear His own words in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
That is not a promise that sin does not matter.
It is a promise about the welcome of the Savior.
Come to Him.
Not with a carefully edited version of your life.
Not with religious performances meant to impress Him.
Come with repentance.
Come with faith.
Come admitting what is true.
He already knows.
And His mercy is not exhausted by your need.
You may need to confess a sin you have hidden.
You may need to seek help from a trustworthy pastor, counselor, or mature believer.
You may need to make restitution for something you have done.
You may need to leave an unsafe situation and seek appropriate protection.
You may need to forgive someone while still maintaining necessary boundaries.
The next faithful step will not look identical for everyone.
But the invitation to turn toward Christ remains.
And perhaps, today, that is where your own story begins to change.
Not because your past was insignificant.
Not because the consequences vanished.
But because Jesus Christ is greater than the darkness you thought would define you forever.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin deserves celebration.
But because the grace of God can reach into the ruins of human lives and bring repentance, forgiveness, restoration, and transformation.
And this message is not something we want to keep behind closed doors.
There are people reading Facebook tonight who have not opened a Bible in years.
People who feel disqualified from approaching God.
People who are quietly struggling with shame, grief, addiction, spiritual exhaustion, or questions they are afraid to ask in church.
Some of them will never search for a Christian teaching page on their own.
But they might read an article shared by someone they trust.
That is why sharing matters.
Not merely to increase the reach of a page.
But because someone in your circle may need to encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
You do not have to share details you are not ready to make public.
Sometimes a few honest words can remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
Your story may encourage someone who has nearly given up.
Return to the Scriptures.
Examine the passages in their contexts.
Do not take even a moving article as a substitute for personally reading God's Word.
And for those who want to help sustain this work more directly, there is another way to participate.
Gospel Warrior is building a growing place for biblical learning, encouragement, and discipleship.
These resources are offered freely because spiritual nourishment should not be reserved only for those who can afford to pay.
But keeping a ministry active, developing resources, preparing biblical content, and expanding its reach require time, effort, and practical support.
Scripture teaches us in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not a transaction for spiritual blessing.
But willing partnership in sharing the Gospel.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Jesus Christ is not a reward reserved for financial supporters.
His invitation to repent and believe is freely proclaimed.

You can glorify God through prayer, obedience, generosity, faithful service, sharing biblical truth, caring for those in need, and countless quiet acts of love that may never receive public recognition.
But only Jesus Christ saves a soul.
And that brings us back to the question with which we began.
Why did the Law protect an escaped slave from being returned to his master?
The passage does not give us an explicit explanation of every reason behind the command.
Its precise scope has been debated.
But its words establish something that should not be overlooked.
The vulnerable fugitive addressed by the law was not to be handed over.
He was permitted to dwell within the community.
He was allowed to choose his place.
He was not to be oppressed.
Within the larger biblical story, this command resonates with Israel's memory of deliverance and God's repeated concern for those exposed to injustice.
And it points us toward a serious responsibility.

If we claim to know the God who delivered Israel from Egypt, and the Savior who announced good news to the poor and freedom to the captives, we cannot be indifferent to the suffering of people made in His image.
We cannot celebrate our own forgiveness while withholding compassion from everyone else.
We cannot preach liberty in Christ while treating people as though they are beyond the reach of His mercy.
And we cannot claim to love Jesus while refusing to hear His call to repentance, holiness, justice, and sacrificial love.
The fugitive in Deuteronomy needed a place where he would not be surrendered to his master.
The sinner needs something even greater.
A Redeemer who can forgive guilt, break the dominion of sin, reconcile us to God, and give us a new life.
That Redeemer is Jesus Christ.
So if you have been running from Him, turn around.
If you have been hiding your sin, confess it.
If you have been treating someone else without mercy, repent.
If you have been crushed beneath the weight of your past, look to the crucified and risen Savior.
And if you have already experienced His grace, become the kind of person through whom others can see His compassion.
Because the most beautiful testimony is not simply that you escaped something terrible.
It is that the mercy of God has begun to make you someone new.
Your past may explain the chains you once carried, but it does not have the authority to overrule the freedom Jesus Christ gives.
